Patient: a 38-year-old Hispanic woman.
Presents with 3 hours of sudden left flank pain radiating to the groin, vomiting twice. Pacing the room, unable to sit still, grimacing. HR 104, BP 142/88. Urinalysis shows blood. No known drug allergies. No history of substance use.

- 3 hours duration
- Vomiting twice
- Pacing the room, unable to sit still (classic for renal colic - patients cannot find a comfortable position)
- Grimacing
- Tachycardia (HR 104) and mild hypertension (BP 142/88) - consistent with severe pain
- Hematuria on urinalysis - confirms urological cause
- No drug allergies, no substance use history

Pain severity assessment: The clinical picture is classic for renal colic. She is pacing, unable to sit still, grimacing, has tachycardia and elevated BP. Renal colic is known as one of the most severe pains a person can experience. The behavioral signs (pacing, inability to find comfort, grimacing) plus autonomic signs (tachycardia, hypertension) suggest severe pain. I'd assess this as 8-9/10. Let me go with 9 - the combination of all these signs points to very severe pain.

- NSAIDs (non-opioid) like ketorolac are first-line for renal colic
- However, with pain this severe (9/10), non-opioid alone may not be sufficient
- Weak opioids (codeine, tramadol) are insufficient for this level of pain
- Strong opioids (morphine, fentanyl, hydromorphone) are appropriate for severe renal colic when NSAIDs alone are inadequate
